/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
from numpy.polynomial.legendre import leggauss
v=np.array([[.13,.21,.31],[.72,.28,.49],[.37,.84,.65]])
xi=np.array([1.3,2.1,-.7])
def data(v):
    e=np.array([v[(p-1)%3]-v[(p+1)%3] for p in range(3)])
    n=np.cross(e[2],e[0]); area=np.linalg.norm(n)/2
    q=e@xi; z=np.exp(-1j*(v@xi))
    f=sum(z[p]/(q[(p-1)%3]*q[(p+1)%3]) for p in range(3))
    return e,n/(2*area),area,q,z,f
def ft(v):
    _,_,a,_,_,f=data(v)
    return 2*a*f
e,n,a,q,z,f=data(v)
grad=[]
for p in range(3):
    m=(p-1)%3; h=(p+1)%3
    df=xi*(z[h]/(q[m]**2*q[p])-z[m]/(q[p]*q[h]**2)-1j*z[p]/(q[m]*q[h])+z[p]/(q[m]**2*q[h])-z[p]/(q[m]*q[h]**2))
    grad.append(-f*np.cross(e[p],n)+2*a*df)
grad=np.array(grad)
fd=np.zeros((3,3),dtype=complex)
for p in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        dv=np.zeros((3,3));dv[p,j]=1e-6
        fd[p,j]=(ft(v+dv)-ft(v-dv))/2e-6
x,w=leggauss(40); x=(x+1)/2;w=w/2
quad=0j
for s,ws in zip(x,w):
    for t,wt in zip(x,w):
        point=v[0]+s*(v[1]-v[0])+(1-s)*t*(v[2]-v[0])
        quad+=ws*wt*2*a*(1-s)*np.exp(-1j*(point@xi))
def g(s):
    return sum(-np.exp(1j*s[p])/((s[p]-s[(p+1)%3])*(s[p]-s[(p-1)%3])) for p in range(3))
print('Eq. 7-8 FT vs numerical surface quadrature absolute error:',abs(ft(v)-quad))
print('Eq. 9-10 gradient vs central finite difference max absolute error:',np.max(np.abs(grad-fd)))
print('Eq. 8 f:',f)
print('Eq. 11 using stated edge arguments and exponent:',g(e@xi))
print('Eq. 11 corrected to vertex arguments and negative exponent:',np.conj(g(v@xi)))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import cmath,math
v=[[.13,.21,.31],[.72,.28,.49],[.37,.84,.65]]
xi=[1.3,2.1,-.7]
def sub(a,b):return [x-y for x,y in zip(a,b)]
def dot(a,b):return sum(x*y for x,y in zip(a,b))
def cross(a,b):return [a[1]*b[2]-a[2]*b[1],a[2]*b[0]-a[0]*b[2],a[0]*b[1]-a[1]*b[0]]
def data(v):
    e=[sub(v[(p-1)%3],v[(p+1)%3]) for p in range(3)]
    n=cross(e[2],e[0]);area=math.sqrt(dot(n,n))/2;n=[x/(2*area) for x in n]
    q=[dot(edge,xi) for edge in e];z=[cmath.exp(-1j*dot(p,xi)) for p in v]
    f=sum(z[p]/(q[(p-1)%3]*q[(p+1)%3]) for p in range(3))
    return e,n,area,q,z,f
def ft(v):
    _,_,a,_,_,f=data(v)
    return 2*a*f
e,n,a,q,z,f=data(v)
grad=[]
for p in range(3):
    m=(p-1)%3;h=(p+1)%3
    df=z[h]/(q[m]**2*q[p])-z[m]/(q[p]*q[h]**2)-1j*z[p]/(q[m]*q[h])+z[p]/(q[m]**2*q[h])-z[p]/(q[m]*q[h]**2)
    normal=cross(e[p],n)
    grad.append([-f*normal[j]+2*a*df*xi[j] for j in range(3)])
errs=[]
for p in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        vp=[r[:] for r in v];vm=[r[:] for r in v]
        vp[p][j]+=1e-6;vm[p][j]-=1e-6
        errs.append(abs(grad[p][j]-(ft(vp)-ft(vm))/2e-6))
quad=0j;nquad=400
for k in range(nquad):
    s=(k+.5)/nquad
    for l in range(nquad):
        t=(l+.5)/nquad
        point=[v[0][j]+s*(v[1][j]-v[0][j])+(1-s)*t*(v[2][j]-v[0][j]) for j in range(3)]
        quad+=2*a*(1-s)*cmath.exp(-1j*dot(point,xi))/(nquad*nquad)
def g(s,sign=1):
    return sum(-cmath.exp(sign*1j*s[p])/((s[p]-s[(p+1)%3])*(s[p]-s[(p-1)%3])) for p in range(3))
print('Eq. 7-8 FT vs numerical surface quadrature absolute error:',abs(ft(v)-quad))
print('Eq. 9-10 gradient vs central finite difference max absolute error:',max(errs))
print('Eq. 8 f:',f)
print('Eq. 11 using stated edge arguments and exponent:',g([dot(edge,xi) for edge in e]))
print('Eq. 11 corrected to vertex arguments and negative exponent:',g([dot(p,xi) for p in v],-1))
PY"

  "strengths": [
    "deltaMic addresses a meaningful computer vision problem: recovering explicit cell surfaces from volumetric fluorescence images without annotated training data. Jointly fitting geometry and microscope blur is a useful formulation, and the resulting meshes could support downstream geometric and biophysical analysis.",
    "The surface-density formulation, analytic triangle Fourier transform and vertex derivatives provide a concrete technical foundation. Custom CUDA kernels and PSF-dependent frequency truncation are well-motivated approaches to accelerating the renderer.",
    "Experiments demonstrate feasibility across several synthetic shapes and mouse, ascidian and worm embryos acquired with different microscopy modalities. On 15 organoid images, Figure 9 reports substantially better image agreement than DM3D, including MSE of 0.0020 versus 0.0125.",
    "The manuscript references a versioned implementation archive, credits experimental data providers and relevant methods, and meaningfully acknowledges limitations involving spatially varying PSFs and computational cost."
  ],
  "weaknesses": [
    "The main acceptance concern is that accurate cell geometry is not independently validated. Sections 6.2–6.3 primarily evaluate rendered-image agreement, although ground-truth meshes are available for the synthetic experiments. The DM3D comparison also renders both methods using deltaMic's inferred PSF. These results establish improved image fitting, but do not establish more accurate surfaces, particularly when blur can conceal geometric errors. Surface-distance measurements on synthetic meshes and independent geometric or segmentation evaluation on real data are needed to substantiate the central claim.",
    "Evidence for joint PSF recovery and broad robustness is limited. Section 6.1 uses the same Gaussian PSF for generation and inference, while the real-data experiments provide neither calibrated PSF references nor parameter-recovery measurements. There is no learned-versus-fixed PSF ablation. Initialization and noise experiments concentrate on one synthetic shape, without adequately specifying the noise model or repeated-trial variability. Performance under nonuniform membrane fluorescence or PSF mismatch remains unclear.",
    "The claim of avoiding shape regularization needs careful qualification and experimental isolation. Section 5.1 applies Laplacian-based gradient smoothing with lambda = 50, and the embryo experiments additionally use remeshing and collision handling. This is compatible with having no explicit regularization penalty in the objective, but the experiments do not establish how much smoothness and robustness come from the rendering model versus these mechanisms. Ablations and sensitivity measurements would clarify the contribution.",
    "Several mathematical inconsistencies impede faithful reimplementation. In Section 3.2, the Fourier transform of a Gaussian with covariance Sigma should use exp(-xi^T Sigma xi / 2), rather than Sigma inverse. Section 4.1.3 expresses f_T using edge projections, whereas the divided-difference expression requires vertex projections; Equation 11 also uses positive exponential phases inconsistent with Equations 8 and 12. The 'equivalent' linear system in Section 5.1 reverses the stated preconditioning operation. These may be correctable transcription errors rather than implementation failures, but corrected formulas and numerical validation near degenerate frequency configurations are necessary.",
    "Practical scalability and reproducibility are incompletely established. Figure 6 benchmarks an 80-triangle mesh across image sizes and triangle-count scaling at 100^3 voxels, whereas applications require thousands of vertices and 1,000–10,000 optimization steps. End-to-end reconstruction times and peak memory at actual experimental resolutions are missing. Learning rates, the shape/PSF update schedule and numerical switching thresholds are also insufficiently specified in the supplied manuscript. The implementation citation is helpful, but the reported evidence does not yet substantiate practical scalability."
  ]

strengths: deltaMic addresses a meaningful computer vision problem: recovering explicit cell surfaces from volumetric fluorescence images without annotated training data. Jointly fitting geometry and microscope blur is a useful formulation, and the resulting meshes could support downstream geometric and biophysical analysis.

The surface-density formulation, analytic triangle Fourier transform and vertex derivatives provide a concrete technical foundation. Custom CUDA kernels and PSF-dependent frequency truncation are well-motivated approaches to accelerating the renderer.

Experiments demonstrate feasibility across several synthetic shapes and mouse, ascidian and worm embryos acquired with different microscopy modalities. On 15 organoid images, Figure 9 reports substantially better image agreement than DM3D, including MSE of 0.0020 versus 0.0125.

The manuscript references a versioned implementation archive, credits experimental data providers and relevant methods, and meaningfully acknowledges limitations involving spatially varying PSFs and computational cost.
weaknesses: The main acceptance concern is that accurate cell geometry is not independently validated. Sections 6.2–6.3 primarily evaluate rendered-image agreement, although ground-truth meshes are available for the synthetic experiments. The DM3D comparison also renders both methods using deltaMic's inferred PSF. These results establish improved image fitting, but do not establish more accurate surfaces, particularly when blur can conceal geometric errors. Surface-distance measurements on synthetic meshes and independent geometric or segmentation evaluation on real data are needed to substantiate the central claim.

Evidence for joint PSF recovery and broad robustness is limited. Section 6.1 uses the same Gaussian PSF for generation and inference, while the real-data experiments provide neither calibrated PSF references nor parameter-recovery measurements. There is no learned-versus-fixed PSF ablation. Initialization and noise experiments concentrate on one synthetic shape, without adequately specifying the noise model or repeated-trial variability. Performance under nonuniform membrane fluorescence or PSF mismatch remains unclear.

The claim of avoiding shape regularization needs careful qualification and experimental isolation. Section 5.1 applies Laplacian-based gradient smoothing with lambda = 50, and the embryo experiments additionally use remeshing and collision handling. This is compatible with having no explicit regularization penalty in the objective, but the experiments do not establish how much smoothness and robustness come from the rendering model versus these mechanisms. Ablations and sensitivity measurements would clarify the contribution.

Several mathematical inconsistencies impede faithful reimplementation. In Section 3.2, the Fourier transform of a Gaussian with covariance Sigma should use exp(-xi^T Sigma xi / 2), rather than Sigma inverse. Section 4.1.3 expresses f_T using edge projections, whereas the divided-difference expression requires vertex projections; Equation 11 also uses positive exponential phases inconsistent with Equations 8 and 12. The 'equivalent' linear system in Section 5.1 reverses the stated preconditioning operation. These may be correctable transcription errors rather than implementation failures, but corrected formulas and numerical validation near degenerate frequency configurations are necessary.

Practical scalability and reproducibility are incompletely established. Figure 6 benchmarks an 80-triangle mesh across image sizes and triangle-count scaling at 100^3 voxels, whereas applications require thousands of vertices and 1,000–10,000 optimization steps. End-to-end reconstruction times and peak memory at actual experimental resolutions are missing. Learning rates, the shape/PSF update schedule and numerical switching thresholds are also insufficiently specified in the supplied manuscript. The implementation citation is helpful, but the reported evidence does not yet substantiate practical scalability.
